questions.q: What is the difference between a declaration and a definition in C++?
options: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
A declaration tells the compiler a name and signature exist; a definition provides the actual implementation
A declaration is only valid in a .cpp file; a definition is only valid in a header
A definition is optional if the program never calls the function
questions.explain: A declaration introduces a name and its type/signature without an implementation. A definition provides that implementation (a function body, or storage). Every definition is also a declaration, but not vice versa.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, what belongs in a header file versus a .cpp file?
options: Definitions go in headers, declarations go in .cpp files
Declarations go in headers, definitions go in .cpp files
Both always go in the same .cpp file
Headers may only contain comments
questions.explain: The standard pattern is: headers hold declarations shared across multiple .cpp files, and .cpp files hold the actual definitions (with some exceptions like templates and inline functions).

It prevents a header's contents from being processed more than once per translation unit, avoiding duplicate declarations
It automatically generates documentation
It enables optimization flags
questions.explain: #pragma once tells the preprocessor to skip a header's contents if it has already been included once in the current translation unit, preventing errors from duplicate declarations (e.g. redeclaring the same struct).

questions.q: A linker reports 'undefined reference to fair_value(double, double, double)'. What does this most likely mean?
options: The function was called but its definition was never compiled or linked in
The function's return type is wrong
The program has a syntax error in main()
The header file is missing a semicolon
questions.explain: Undefined reference means the linker found a call to a function but no matching definition in any object file it linked — typically a missing source file, a typo, or a signature mismatch.

questions.q: What typically causes a 'multiple definition' linker error?
options: Forgetting to include a header
A full function body (not just a declaration) sitting in a header without protection, included into two different .cpp files
Using #pragma once
Declaring a function with default arguments
questions.explain: If a complete function definition lives in a header and that header is included by multiple .cpp files, each resulting object file contains its own copy of the definition, and the linker refuses to combine them.
